subject: psychology
topic: You judge a face in a tenth of a second
angle: People form trait impressions from faces in as little as 100 milliseconds, though these impressions can be learned and may differ from those formed from voices.
title: The 100 Millisecond Judgment

hooks.text: How fast do you judge a stranger?
You think you are being objective. You are not.
You are making life-altering decisions in a blink.
A face appears. A judgment follows. In a tenth of a second.

reveal.headline: You judge a person in 100 milliseconds.
reveal.body: First impressions of traits from faces occur in as little as 100 ms. These judgments correlate with those made without time limits.

explain.headline: Your brain processes faces faster than speech.
explain.body: Trait impressions from faces form in 100 ms. Impressions from voices take longer, stabilizing by 400 ms. Longer exposure to faces can lead to more negative judgments.

matters.headline: Visual bias dictates your reality.
matters.body: That may be why your first glance at a stranger dictates your trust in them. Your brain makes a decision before you have time to think.

example.headline: The hallway at your office.
example.body: You pass a colleague in the corridor. You decide if they are competent or approachable before they can say a single word to you.

question.headline: Who are you judging right now?

stat.label: of Senate races in 2004 predicted by facial appearance

claims.text: Inferences of competence based solely on facial appearance predicted the outcomes of U.S. congressional elections better than chance (e.g., 68.8% of the Senate races in 2004).
claims.quote: We show that inferences of competence based solely on facial appearance predicted the outcomes of U.S. congressional elections better than chance (e.g., 68.8% of the Senate races in 2004)

claims.text: Once learned, first impressions occur following very brief exposure (100 ms).
claims.quote: Crucially, in the final two experiments (Experiments 4 and 5) we show that, once learned, these first impressions occur following very brief exposure (100 ms).

claims.text: Judgments made after a 100-ms exposure to a face correlated highly with judgments made in the absence of time constraints.
claims.quote: Judgments made after a 100-ms exposure correlated highly with judgments made in the absence of time constraints, suggesting that this exposure time was sufficient for participants to form an impression.

claims.text: Trait impressions from voices require longer exposure to develop and stabilize although they are still formed by 400 ms.
claims.quote: Unlike faces, however, trait impressions from voices require longer exposure to develop and stabilize although they are still formed by 400 ms.

claims.text: When exposure time increased from 100 to 500 ms, participants' judgments became more negative, response times for judgments decreased, and confidence in judgments increased.
claims.quote: When exposure time increased from 100 to 500 ms, participants' judgments became more negative, response times for judgments decreased, and confidence in judgments increased.

verdict: The evidence confirms that trait inferences from faces occur rapidly, often within 100 milliseconds, and can influence real-world behaviors like voting.
caveat: While impressions are formed rapidly, increasing exposure time can lead to more negative judgments and more differentiated person impressions.
caption:
Your brain makes snap judgments about others before you are even aware of them.

Research shows that trait impressions from faces occur in 100 ms and can influence real-world behaviors like voting. However, as exposure time increases, these judgments can become more negative and confident.

How many people have you judged today without speaking to them?
